reference.source: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery / Sabiston Textbook of Surgery
clinicalPearls: Fibroadenoma is the commonest benign solid breast lump in young women, typically presenting as a smooth, firm, well-defined, highly mobile mass, hence the nickname breast mouse
It is usually painless and often discovered incidentally; multiple and bilateral lesions occur in a minority
Assessment follows triple assessment: clinical examination, imaging (ultrasound in younger women, with mammography added in older patients), and needle biopsy where indicated
Ultrasound characteristically shows a well-circumscribed, hypoechoic, oval lesion with a benign appearance
Core biopsy is used to confirm the diagnosis and, importantly, to distinguish a fibroadenoma from a phyllodes tumour, which can behave more aggressively

Many small, biopsy-proven fibroadenomas can be safely observed, as a proportion regress, while excision is offered for large, enlarging, symptomatic, or diagnostically uncertain lesions or patient preference
A giant fibroadenoma or a rapidly enlarging lesion should prompt careful exclusion of a phyllodes tumour
reference.pathophysiology: A fibroadenoma is a benign biphasic tumour arising from the breast lobule, composed of both epithelial and stromal (fibrous) elements that proliferate together. It is regarded as an aberration of normal breast development and involution rather than a true neoplasm, and its growth is hormonally responsive, which explains its predominance in the reproductive years, occasional enlargement during pregnancy, and tendency to regress after the menopause. The lesion is well encapsulated and mobile within the breast tissue. The main clinical distinction is from phyllodes tumours, which share stromal and epithelial components but have greater stromal cellularity and a spectrum of behaviour from benign to malignant.
additionalDifferentials: Lipoma or other benign stromal lesion
additionalInvestigations: Breast ultrasound as first-line imaging in younger women
Mammography in older patients or where imaging is indeterminate
Core needle biopsy for histological confirmation and to exclude phyllodes tumour or malignancy
Fine-needle aspiration cytology in selected settings as part of triple assessment
Clinical follow-up imaging for lesions managed conservatively
redFlags: Rapid growth or a large (giant) lesion suggesting a phyllodes tumour
Irregular, hard, or fixed features or suspicious imaging raising concern for malignancy
New solid breast mass in an older woman requiring careful exclusion of cancer
Discordance between clinical, imaging, and pathology findings on triple assessment
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is excellent; fibroadenomas are benign, a significant proportion regress or remain stable, and they carry little or no increase in subsequent breast cancer risk in the usual simple form. Recurrence after complete excision is uncommon, though new fibroadenomas may develop elsewhere.
pitfalls: Assuming a solid mass in an older woman is a fibroadenoma without excluding carcinoma
Failing to distinguish a phyllodes tumour from a fibroadenoma, leading to inadequate excision margins
Ignoring discordance within triple assessment and falsely reassuring the patient
Over-treating small, biopsy-proven, asymptomatic fibroadenomas that could be safely observed
Neglecting follow-up of a lesion managed conservatively that later enlarges
references: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
